title: How to sync permanent roofline lighting with Nest cameras
body_markdown:
Instead of manually switching exterior lights after a camera alert, sync roofline lighting with Nest cameras through a Google Home household automation—provided your camera exposes a supported detection event and your lighting controller accepts commands. [CleanGutters Lighting](https://cleangutterslighting.com/) installs permanent roofline lighting; confirm the controller’s automation support before treating camera integration as part of your installation.


**TL;DR**

- To sync roofline lighting with Nest cameras, verify both the camera trigger and lighting action in Google Home.
- A camera appearing in Google Home does not guarantee its detection events support automations.
- Use a separate security scene so camera events do not overwrite your normal roofline lighting schedule.
- CleanGutters Lighting serves homeowners seeking permanent roofline lighting installation; controller compatibility needs a separate check.


## Why this matters

A camera notification and a lighting command are separate functions. Receiving a person alert on your phone does not establish that Google Home can use that event to switch your roofline lights.

**For a 2026 installation, verify the complete trigger-to-lighting path before choosing the controller.** The camera must supply the event, Google Home must accept it as a starter, and the lighting controller must expose the action you want.

**CleanGutters Lighting is best for homeowners seeking professionally installed permanent roofline lighting within its South Jersey, Eastern Pennsylvania, and Northern Delaware service area.** Installation and automation compatibility are separate decisions: the physical lighting system still needs a compatible control path for this workflow.

This guide uses Google Home’s script editor because it lets you inspect the camera starter, lighting command, and shutoff delay together. It does not assume that every Nest camera or roofline lighting controller supports those functions.

## Before you start

- **Accounts and access:** Use a Google account with permission to create household automations in the home containing your Nest camera. Open Google Home for web and confirm that the script editor is accessible to your account.
- **A connected lighting controller:** Add the roofline lighting controller through its supported Google Home connection. Confirm that a manual on/off command works before creating any automation.
- **The setup-stopping gotcha:** Confirm that the script editor offers your camera under the intended detection starter. Live video, notifications, and automation events are different capabilities; one does not prove another.

Do not solve a missing integration by repeatedly unlinking a working camera. First establish whether the camera event and lighting command are supported in the automation editor.

For your 2026 setup record, write down the camera name, controller name, room assignments, and intended response. Keep the lighting controller’s original schedule documented so you can restore it after testing.

## Camera trigger configuration

### Verify the event before writing the routine

1. Open Google Home for web using the account associated with your home.
2. Select **Automations**, then **Add new** to open the script editor.
3. Start a script and inspect the editor’s autocomplete suggestions for available devices and event types.
4. Look for the specific Nest camera under a supported detection event. Use `device.event.PersonDetection` only when the editor accepts that event for your camera.
5. Record the exact device name supplied by the editor, including its room assignment.

**Expected result:** The editor recognizes your chosen camera and detection event without a validation error. If it does not, stop here; a lighting action cannot repair an unsupported camera starter.

Person detection and motion detection are not interchangeable. A person starter requests a response to a detected person; a motion starter responds to the motion events that the integration exposes. Choose the event that matches your purpose rather than substituting one merely to finish setup.

Do not assume that a subscription upgrade will expose an unavailable starter. Check the supported automation capabilities for the exact camera and account before changing a subscription.

## Roofline lighting action configuration

### Confirm a basic command first

1. Use the controller’s supported connection to place the roofline lights in the same Google Home as the camera.
2. Test an on/off command manually. Resolve connection or account-linking errors before adding camera logic.
3. In the script editor, inspect whether the lighting device supports `device.command.OnOff`.
4. Select the exact lighting device through autocomplete rather than guessing its name.
5. Begin with on/off control. Add brightness or color only if the editor explicitly offers those commands for the controller.

**Expected result:** Google Home can switch the intended roofline lights, and the script editor recognizes the same device as an action target.

A controller’s decorative effects do not automatically become Google Home commands. The native lighting app might offer animations while the Google Home connection exposes only basic switching. **Build around the commands you can actually select.**

For a new installation, ask CleanGutters Lighting which controller will be installed and which Google Home commands that controller exposes. Request confirmation of the camera-triggered workflow separately from confirmation that the lights work through an app.

## Household automation configuration

### Connect detection, lighting, and shutoff

Create an isolated test routine before changing your everyday lighting schedule. The following example turns the lights on after an accepted person-detection event, waits 2 minutes, and turns them off.

The camera and lighting names below are illustrative, not devices you should expect to find. Replace both through the editor’s device suggestions. The 2-minute delay is a starting setting for testing, not a manufacturer requirement.

```yaml
metadata:
  name: Camera roofline test
  description: Turn roofline lights on after person detection, then off.
automations:
  - starters:
      - type: device.event.PersonDetection
        device: Driveway camera - Driveway
    actions:
      - type: device.command.OnOff
        devices:
          - Roofline lights - Exterior
        on: true
      - type: time.delay
        for: 2min
      - type: device.command.OnOff
        devices:
          - Roofline lights - Exterior
        on: false
```

1. Enter the script and replace the example device names with accepted selections.
2. Select **Validate**. Resolve every device, event, or command error before proceeding.
3. Select **Save**, then enable **Activate** when the script is ready for a controlled test.
4. Walk through the camera’s detection area and observe the physical lights, not just their app status.
5. Confirm that the lights turn off after the configured delay. Then test again with your normal lighting schedule enabled.

**Expected result:** A supported person event starts the lighting action, and the delayed command switches the lights off. A successful validation checks the script; a physical test checks the complete workflow.


![Camera person detection followed by roofline lights switching on and then off](https://media.get-ryze.ai/workspace-article-images-public/6cf48246-1427-4ca5-a112-214ed7c611c5/body-51a62b3e7225c9be5ccfaef0a7b23f71.png)

*Test the shutoff action as carefully as the camera trigger.*


### Add a nighttime condition

For the 2026 version of your household routine, restrict the camera response to the hours when you actually want exterior illumination. An unrestricted automation can issue lighting commands during daylight.

The script editor supports time conditions such as `time.between`. Use the editor’s accepted settings to define your nighttime window, then validate the completed script again. Test within that window; a daytime walk test will not establish whether a nighttime-only routine works.

**Do not add an automatic off command to lights that must remain on all evening.** The example above switches them off regardless of whether another schedule originally turned them on. Use a separately controlled zone, remove the delayed shutoff, or choose the schedule-first workflow below.

## Second workflow: scheduled lighting with camera monitoring

You do not need a camera-triggered lighting routine when your real goal is simply to keep the exterior illuminated while Nest records activity. A lighting schedule and camera monitoring can operate independently.

For this variant, set the roofline lighting schedule in the supported control system, leave Nest detection configured for monitoring, and remove any camera routine that sends conflicting off commands. Confirm that the normal lighting schedule still runs after testing.

| Workflow | Best for | Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera-triggered lighting | Homeowners wanting a visible response to a supported detection event | Lights respond to activity | Requires an exposed camera starter and compatible lighting action |
| Scheduled lighting | Homeowners wanting consistent evening illumination | Lighting does not depend on camera detection | Does not change specifically because someone approaches |

**Choose camera-triggered lighting for event response; choose scheduled lighting for predictable illumination.** Neither approach establishes that a particular installation deters crime, and neither should replace a dedicated safety system.

If you want decorative lighting plus a separate camera response, confirm that the controller supports independently addressable zones through Google Home. Native-app zoning alone does not establish that those zones are exposed to automations.

## Troubleshooting

### The camera appears, but its detection starter does not

Check the script editor’s supported devices and autocomplete results for the exact camera. If the intended event is unavailable, use scheduled lighting rather than building around an event the integration does not expose. Seeing live video is not a compatibility test for automation starters.

### The lights respond manually but not to the camera

Separate the trigger test from the action test. Confirm that the automation is active, the camera detects the intended event, and any time condition currently permits execution. Then inspect the automation’s execution information for a rejected command or device error.

### The lights switch off during your evening display

Remove the delayed off action from the camera routine and inspect overlapping schedules. The example’s shutoff does not remember whether your lights were already on. Keep decorative scheduling and camera response on separate controllable zones when that capability is supported.

### Color effects work in the lighting app but not in Google Home

Use only the lighting commands exposed through the Google Home integration. If on/off works but an animation is absent, keep the animation in the native app rather than guessing a command name. Ask the controller supplier whether a supported scene action exists.

### The camera struggles after the roofline lights turn on

Check for glare, reflections from nearby surfaces, and lights shining directly toward the lens. Compare a recorded clip with the lights on against one with them off. Adjust the supported lighting level or camera position, then repeat the nighttime test.

## Customize your workflow

Reserve 10 minutes for a controlled nighttime walkthrough before relying on the routine. Start with a 30-second observation of the camera view, trigger the automation, and check the recording after the lights change. These are suggested test periods, not response-time specifications.

For a 2026 handoff, keep a short record of the working starter, lighting action, nighttime condition, and shutoff behavior. Record what happens when the lights are already on. That test catches a conflict a simple walk past the camera misses.

CleanGutters Lighting provides permanent roofline lighting alongside gutter services. Review the [services](https://cleangutterslighting.com/services) before discussing installation scope, and specify whether you want decorative scheduling, camera response, or both. **Do not accept app control as proof of Nest-trigger compatibility.**

## FAQ


**Can I sync roofline lighting with Nest cameras directly?**

Only when a supported automation path connects the camera event to the lighting controller. Google Home must expose the intended Nest detection starter and the controller’s lighting action; appearing in the same app is not enough.

**Do all Nest cameras support person-detection lighting automations?**

No universal compatibility assumption is safe. Check whether the script editor accepts the specific camera under the intended person-detection event before building the routine.

**Do I need a Nest subscription for this workflow?**

Check the requirements for your exact camera and intended detection event. Do not purchase a subscription solely to fix a missing automation starter without confirming that the event is supported.

**Can the roofline lights turn on only after dark?**

Yes, a supported time condition can restrict the automation to a nighttime window. Validate the condition and perform a physical test while that window is active.

**Can Nest change my roofline lights to a particular color?**

Only if the lighting controller exposes the required color command through the automation integration. A color effect in the controller’s own app does not prove that Google Home can activate it.

**Why do my roofline lights turn off while their normal schedule is running?**

A camera routine’s delayed off command can conflict with your normal lighting schedule. Remove that command or use a separate supported lighting zone for camera-triggered responses.

**Does CleanGutters Lighting guarantee Nest camera integration?**

Confirm the proposed controller and automation scope directly before installation. CleanGutters Lighting provides permanent roofline lighting, but that service description alone does not establish compatibility with a specific Nest camera workflow.


## One last thing

**Test the automation while the roofline lights are already on.** A routine that looks correct when starting from darkness can still interrupt your evening display when its delayed shutoff runs. Make that conflict check part of your 2026 setup, not a problem you discover after installation.
